title: From a probability to a position
objectives: Turn predicted probabilities into position sizes.
Compare the AFML bet size with Kelly and explain why desks bet a fraction of Kelly.

screens.title: Two trades, one stake
screens.prose: A classifier scores two trades. Trade A wins with probability 0.51 and trade B with 0.9. Each pays £1 per £1 staked if it wins and loses the £1 if not. A rule that buys whenever $p > 0.5$ stakes the same on both.
screens.question: How many times larger is the expected profit per £1 on B than on A?

hints.text: Per £1 staked, you win £1 with chance $p$ and lose £1 with chance $1 - p$.
Read the heights of A and B on the line.
A earns $2 \times 0.51 - 1 = 0.02$ per £1 and B earns $2 \times 0.9 - 1 = 0.8$. Divide the two.

feedback.correct: B earns £0.80 per £1 staked and A earns £0.02.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the expected profit per £1 for each trade, then divide.

byKey.ratio-p: You divided the probabilities. The profit per £1 is $p - (1 - p) = 2p - 1$, not $p$.
byKey.diff: That is the difference in profit. The question asks how many times larger B's profit is.

explain.text: B earns £0.80 per £1 and A earns £0.02, forty times less. A rule that stakes the same on both risks as much capital on a near coin flip as on a strong call. The stake should grow with how sure the model is.

screens.title: A size that grows with confidence
screens.prose: One way to make the size grow with confidence: ask how far $p$ sits from a coin flip, measured in its own spread. The curve maps $p$ to a size from −1, fully short, to 1, fully long. Slide $p$.
screens.question: Set $p = 0.55$. What size does the curve give? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Move the slider to 0.55 and read the caption.
The size is the height of the dot on the curve.
At $p = 0.55$ the caption reads a size of 0.080.

feedback.correct: A 55% call earns a small position, 0.08 of the full size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 0.55 and read the size in the caption.

byKey.kelly: That is $2p - 1 = 0.1$, the edge. The curve sits a little below it near 0.5.
byKey.prob: You read the probability. The size is the height of the curve.

explain.text: At 0.55 the curve gives 0.08, and below 0.5 it turns negative: a short. Near 0.5 it is flat, so weak calls get small sizes. Far from 0.5 it bends towards full size.

screens.title: The test statistic behind the curve
screens.prose: López de Prado's *Advances in Financial Machine Learning* (AFML, chapter 10) builds this curve. Treat the call as a test of $p = \tfrac12$: $$z = \frac{p - \tfrac12}{\sqrt{p(1-p)}}, \qquad m = 2\Phi(z) - 1,$$ with $\Phi$ the standard normal CDF and $m$ the **bet size**.
screens.question: Compute the bet size at $p = 0.7$. Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Start with $p(1 - p) = 0.7 \times 0.3$.
$\Phi(0.436) = 0.669$, so $m = 2 \times 0.669 - 1 = 0.338$. The slider at 0.7 confirms it.

feedback.correct: A 70% call gets about a third of the full size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $z$, then $\Phi(z)$, then $2\Phi(z) - 1$.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(z)$. Double it and subtract 1.
byKey.kelly: That is $2p - 1$, the Kelly stake at even odds. The AFML curve is a different rule.

explain.text: You found $z = 0.436$, so $m = 2\Phi(0.436) - 1 = 0.34$. At $p = 0.5$, $z = 0$ and the size is 0: no edge, no bet. The curve only says how much; the side, long or short, comes from the sign of $p - \tfrac12$.

screens.title: Kelly, when a win pays more
screens.prose: You met Kelly in the conditional course (Bayes on a trading signal). For a bet that wins £$b$ per £1 staked and loses the £1 otherwise, Kelly stakes $$f = p - \frac{1-p}{b}.$$ The dashed line is Kelly; slide the odds $b$.
screens.question: A trade wins £2 per £1 staked ($b = 2$) with probability 0.4. What fraction does Kelly stake?

hints.text: Put $p = 0.4$ and $b = 2$ into the formula.
Set the slider to $b = 2$ and read the dashed line at $p = 0.4$.

feedback.correct: Kelly stakes a tenth of capital.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $p - (1 - p)/b$ with $p = 0.4$ and $b = 2$.

byKey.even: You used the even-odds rule $2p - 1$. Here a win pays £2, so the loss term is divided by 2.
byKey.nobet: A chance below 0.5 can still be worth a bet when a win pays more than a loss costs.
byKey.times-b: You multiplied the loss term by $b$. It is divided by $b$: $0.4 - 0.6/2$.

explain.text: You found $f = 0.4 - 0.3 = 0.1$: a 40% bet paying 2 to 1 has an edge. At even odds, $b = 1$, Kelly is $2p - 1$, which sits above the AFML curve for most $p$.

screens.title: Half Kelly
screens.prose: Kelly maximises the long-run growth of capital, $g(f) = p\ln(1+f) + (1-p)\ln(1-f)$ per even-odds bet. The curve is $g$ for $p = 0.55$, where Kelly is $f = 0.1$. Many desks bet half Kelly.
screens.question: What share of full Kelly's growth does half Kelly keep? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Read the heights of the two points.
Kelly grows 0.501% per bet and half Kelly 0.375%.

feedback.correct: Half Kelly keeps about three quarters of the growth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide half Kelly's growth by full Kelly's.

byKey.half: Halving the stake does not halve the growth. The curve is flat near its top.
byKey.lost: That is the share lost. The question asks for the share kept.

explain.text: Half Kelly keeps 75% of the growth with half the swings in wealth. The curve is flat near its peak, so betting less costs little. Past the peak growth falls fast, and $p$ is only an estimate: that is why desks bet a fraction of Kelly.

screens.title: Flipping on noise
screens.prose: Over four days the model's $p$ reads 0.51, 0.49, 0.52 and 0.48. An all-or-nothing rule goes fully long when $p > 0.5$ and fully short below.
screens.question: Starting flat, how many units does the all-or-nothing rule trade over the four days?

widget.label: Units traded
widget.accept: 7: one unit to enter, then three flips of 2 units each.

hints.text: Going from flat to +1 trades one unit. What does going from +1 to −1 trade?
Each flip sells the long and opens a short: 2 units.
Enter with 1 unit, then flip three times at 2 units each: $1 + 3 \times 2$.

feedback.correct: Seven units of trading for four calls that were all close to a coin flip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the size of each change in position, starting from 0.

byKey.days: You counted one unit a day. A flip from +1 to −1 trades 2 units.
byKey.flips: You counted the flips. Each one trades 2 units, and the entry trades 1.
byKey.six: You left out the first trade, from flat to +1.

explain.text: The rule traded 7 units on four near coin flips. The AFML curve sizes them at about ±0.02 and ±0.03, and rounding to steps of 0.1 makes every one 0: no trades. **Discretising** sizes stops churn; the next lesson prices it.

screens.title: Bets that overlap
screens.prose: Labels last several days, so bets overlap (level 1, Overlapping labels). Bet 1, size 0.4, runs days 0 to 2. Bet 2, size 0.8, runs days 1 to 4. Bet 3, size −0.2, runs days 3 to 5. AFML holds the **average** size of the bets open each day.
screens.question: Fill in the position on days 1, 3 and 5.

hints.text: Average the sizes of the bets open that day.
Day 1 has bets 1 and 2 open: 0.4 and 0.8.

feedback.correct: Averaging keeps the position between −1 and 1 however many bets are open.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On each day, add the sizes of the open bets and divide by how many there are.

explain.text: You averaged the open bets: 0.6 on day 1, 0.3 on day 3 and −0.2 on day 5. Adding them instead would give 1.2 on day 1, more than a full position. Averaging also smooths the position as bets come and go.

screens.title: Sizing on an overconfident model
screens.prose: Your model says $p = 0.6$ on even-odds trades, so Kelly says stake 0.2. A calibration check (statistical learning, Probabilities you can trust) shows trades scored 0.6 win only 55% of the time. The curve is growth for a true 0.55.
screens.question: You stake 0.2 per trade while the true chance is 0.55. What growth do you get?

options.why: You scaled growth with the stake. Past Kelly, growth falls; at twice Kelly it is about zero.

options.text: About zero: the extra size eats the whole edge
The same as staking 0.1, since the edge is the same
options.why: The edge is the same but the swings are bigger. Losses in $\ln(1 - f)$ grow faster than gains.
You took the loss side alone. Wins and losses nearly cancel: growth is about −0.01%.

hints.text: Which point is the model's stake, and where does it sit on the true curve?
The model's stake is twice the true Kelly fraction.
Read the height at $f = 0.2$: $0.55\ln 1.2 + 0.45\ln 0.8 \approx -0.0001$.

feedback.correct: An overconfident $p$ doubled the stake and wiped out the growth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the true growth curve at $f = 0.2$.

byKey.double: You assumed growth rises with the stake. Kelly is the peak: twice Kelly grows at about zero, so the bigger bet earned nothing.

explain.text: At $f = 0.2$ with a true 0.55, $g = 0.55\ln 1.2 + 0.45\ln 0.8 = -0.0001$: about zero. The model's overconfidence doubled the size, and double Kelly grows at about nothing. Size depends on $p$, so calibrate $p$ before you size.

screens.title: Where $2p - 1$ comes from
screens.prose: Kelly picks the stake $f$ that maximises the expected log growth of one even-odds bet. Derive it.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $g(f) = p\ln(1+f) + (1-p)\ln(1-f)$: a win multiplies capital by $1 + f$, a loss by $1 - f$
$g'(f) = \dfrac{p}{1+f} - \dfrac{1-p}{1-f} = 0$: the slope is zero at the peak
$p - pf = 1 - p + f - pf$: expand both brackets

hints.text: Start from the quantity Kelly maximises.
At a maximum the derivative is zero; clear the fractions next.
Order: growth, derivative set to zero, clear fractions, expand, solve.

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the growth first, differentiate, then solve for $f$.

byKey.m: Clearing the fractions needs the fractions first: the derivative line comes before it.
byKey.f: The answer comes last, after the expansion.

explain.text: Setting $g'(f) = 0$ and clearing fractions gives $p - pf = 1 - p + f - pf$, so $f = 2p - 1$. With odds $b$ the same steps give $f = p - (1-p)/b$. Since $g''(f) < 0$, this is a maximum.

screens.title: Sizing rules in code
screens.prose: Now in code. Use `math.erf` for $\Phi$: $\Phi(z) = \tfrac12\left(1 + \operatorname{erf}(z/\sqrt2)\right)$. `fractional_kelly` returns 0 when Kelly is negative: no bet.
screens.question: Complete `bet_size_from_prob(p)`, `kelly_fraction(p, b)` and `fractional_kelly(p, b, frac)`.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests, including $p = 0.5$, a short ($p = 0.3$) and a negative Kelly. Each result is rounded and accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: $2\Phi(z) - 1$ simplifies: $2 \cdot \tfrac12(1 + \operatorname{erf}(z/\sqrt2)) - 1 = \operatorname{erf}(z/\sqrt2)$.
`kelly_fraction` is one line: `p - (1 - p) / b`.
`fractional_kelly` returns `max(0.0, frac * kelly_fraction(p, b))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your output with the expected values above and check the case of a negative Kelly.

explain.text: The AFML size is $2\Phi(z) - 1 = \operatorname{erf}(z/\sqrt 2)$, so one call does it. Kelly is one line, and the fractional version floors a negative Kelly at 0 rather than betting the other way at the same odds.

screens.title: Rounding and averaging in code
screens.prose: Two more pieces. `discretise` rounds a size to the nearest multiple of `step`. `average_active_bets` returns one position per day: the mean size of the bets open that day, or 0 when none is. A bet is open from its start day to its end day, both included.
screens.question: Complete `discretise(size, step)` and `average_active_bets(sizes, starts, ends, n_days)`.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: five roundings and four sets of overlapping bets, including days with no bet open. Results are rounded and accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: `round(size / step)` counts whole steps; multiply back by `step`.
Collect the sizes with `a <= t <= b` by zipping the three lists.
Append `sum(open_sizes) / len(open_sizes)`, or 0.0 when the list is empty.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check days with no bet open, and that both end days are included.

explain.text: Rounding to whole steps turns tiny changes in $p$ into no trade at all. Averaging the open bets keeps the position in $[-1, 1]$ and lets it change gradually as bets start and end.

screens.title: The desk's sizing table
screens.prose: A desk trades even-odds bets from a calibrated model. Its sizing table maps $p = 0.58$ to a position of 0.3 and $p = 0.65$ to 0.6. The risk team asks how this compares with Kelly.
screens.question: At $p = 0.65$, the desk's position is how many times the Kelly fraction?

hints.text: Kelly at even odds is $2p - 1$.
Kelly at 0.65 is 0.3. Compare the desk's 0.6 with it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the desk's 0.6 by the Kelly fraction at $p = 0.65$.

byKey.afml: You compared with the AFML size, 0.247. The question asks about Kelly, $2p - 1 = 0.3$.
byKey.prob: You divided by $p$. Kelly at even odds is $2p - 1$.

explain.text: Kelly at 0.65 is 0.3, so the desk bets twice Kelly; at 0.58 it bets 1.9 times. At double Kelly, growth is $0.65\ln 1.6 + 0.35\ln 0.4 = -1.5\%$ per bet, against $+4.6\%$ at Kelly. A cap on size whatever $p$ says, set by risk, guards against tables like this.

ideas: A size should grow with confidence: AFML maps $p$ to $m = 2\Phi(z) - 1$ with $z = (p - \tfrac12)/\sqrt{p(1-p)}$, so $p = 0.5$ gives 0.
Kelly stakes $f = p - (1-p)/b$, or $2p - 1$ at even odds. Desks bet a fraction of it because $p$ is estimated and growth falls fast past Kelly.
The position is side times size, averaged over the open bets and rounded to steps so that noise in $p$ does not churn the book.

formula.name: AFML bet size
formula.note: Only as good as $p$: calibrate before you size.

summary.trap: Sizing on an overconfident $p$: a model that says 0.6 when the truth is 0.55 bets double Kelly and grows at about zero.

quiz.prose: Your model outputs $p = 1.00$ for one trade. The AFML curve says full size.
quiz.question: What should you conclude?

options.text: Bet full size: the model is sure
options.why: A probability of 1 says the trade cannot lose. In a market that points to a leak or overfitting, not certainty.

options.text: The model is almost surely leaking or overfit: check it before trading
Bet Kelly, $2p - 1 = 1$: all of the capital
options.why: Kelly at $p = 1$ stakes everything. One loss then ends the account, and the model is almost surely wrong.
Size zero belongs to $p = 0.5$, where there is no edge. At $p = 1$ the formula gives full size; the question is whether to trust it.

feedback.correct: No market trade is certain, so a 1.00 is a warning.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $p = 1$ claims about a market outcome.

explain.text: At $p = 1$, $z$ is infinite and the size is full. No trade in a liquid market is certain, so a 1.00 means a feature saw the outcome or the model memorised its training data. Edge case: at $p = 0.5$ the size is 0.

quiz.prose: An even-odds trade has a calibrated $p = 0.6$. The desk bets half Kelly.
quiz.question: What fraction of capital does it stake?

widget.label: Fraction staked
widget.accept: 0.1: Kelly is $2 \times 0.6 - 1 = 0.2$, and half of it is 0.1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find Kelly, $2p - 1$, then halve it.

byKey.full: That is full Kelly. The desk bets half of it.
byKey.halfp: You halved $p$. Halve the Kelly fraction $2p - 1$ instead.

explain.text: Kelly at even odds is $2p - 1 = 0.2$. Half Kelly stakes 0.1, keeping about three quarters of the growth.

quiz.prose: A primary model says short. The meta-label model (level 1, Should I take this trade?) gives $p = 0.8$ that the short works, so the AFML size is 0.547. Risk caps any position at 0.25.
quiz.question: What position do you take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The position is side times size, and the size cannot exceed the cap.

byKey.nocap: You left out the cap. Risk limits the size to 0.25 whatever $p$ says.
byKey.long: The primary model said short, so the side is −1.

explain.text: The side comes from the primary model and the size from $p$: $-1 \times \min(0.547, 0.25) = -0.25$. The cap binds whenever the model is confident, which is when an error would cost most.

quiz.prose: The model moves from $p = 0.62$ to $p = 0.63$. The AFML sizes are 0.195 and 0.219. The desk rounds sizes to steps of 0.1.
quiz.question: How much does the position change?

feedback.correct: Both round to 0.2, so nothing trades.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round each size to the nearest 0.1, then compare.

byKey.raw: That is the change before rounding. Both sizes round to 0.2.
byKey.step: Both sizes round to the same step, 0.2.

explain.text: 0.195 and 0.219 both round to 0.2, so the position stays put. Rounding absorbs small changes in $p$ that would otherwise turn into trades and costs.
